Functional Traits We gathered data on body size and dispersal ability for each arthropod species studied.

For all arthropods, the traits analyzed were the following: the trophic guild (herbivorous, predators, fungivores, detritivores, and coprophagous organisms), how arthropods ingest food, e.g., feeding behaviors (piercing/sucking, chewing/cutting, and external digestion and sucking), some ecological traits, such as the daily activity (diurnal, nocturnal or active during twilight), the dispersal abilities (high or low dispersal abilities), and the standardized body size.
Finally, for beetles, specific traits were gathered regarding their color and presence or absence of iridescence (Table 1).

Body size standardization was applied for each order present in our samples for analyses, considering all arthropods as follows: $$ \begin{array}{l} \text {Standardized body size of Species} x = (\text {body size of Species} \times \text {Order average} \\ \text {body size}) / \text {Order Standard Deviation body size} \end{array} $$ For beetles, the traits analyzed were the following: the trophic level (herbivorous, predators, fungivores, and detritivores), the beetle’s coloration, the presence or absence of iridescence and some ecological traits, such as the daily activity (diurnal, nocturnal or active during twilight), high dispersal abilities, and the real body size.
Finally, for beetles, specific traits were gathered regarding their color and presence or absence of iridescence (Table 1).

Functional Traits We gathered data on body size and dispersal ability for each arthropod species studied.

For all arthropods, the traits analyzed were the following: the trophic guild (herbivorous, predators, fungivores, detritivores, and coprophagous organisms), how arthropods ingest food, e.g., feeding behaviors (piercing/sucking, chewing/cutting, and external digestion and sucking), some ecological traits, such as the daily activity (diurnal, nocturnal or active during twilight), the dispersal abilities (high or low dispersal abilities), and the standardized body size.
Finally, for beetles, specific traits were gathered regarding their color and presence or absence of iridescence (Table 1).

Body size standardization was applied for each order present in our samples for analyses, considering all arthropods as follows: $$ \begin{array}{l} \text {Standardized body size of Species} x = (\text {body size of Species} \times \text {Order average} \\ \text {body size}) / \text {Order Standard Deviation body size} \end{array} $$ For beetles, the traits analyzed were the following: the trophic level (herbivorous, predators, fungivores, and detritivores), the beetle’s coloration, the presence or absence of iridescence and some ecological traits, such as the daily activity (diurnal, nocturnal or active during twilight), high dispersal abilities, and the real body size.
Finally, for beetles, specific traits were gathered regarding their color and presence or absence of iridescence (Table 1).

basisOfRecord.quote: This in situ study examines the responses of arthropod communities to rising temperatures in intensively managed pastures on the volcanic island of Terceira (Azores, Portugal), employing a functional trait approach.
A field experiment was established using Open Top Chambers (OTCs).
The collected specimens were preserved in 96% ethanol.

All collected arthropods were sorted and identified to the species level when feasible, covering target groups such as Arachnida (Araneae, Opiliones, Pseudoscorpiones), Diplopoda, Chilopoda, and most Insecta groups, including Formicidae and Lepidoptera, but excluding Diptera and Hymenoptera.

lifeStage.quote: Functional traits for each species were determined based on the characteristics of the adult stage.

measurementStatistic.quote: lower abundances of herbivores, coprophagous organisms, detritivores, and fungivores at high elevations in summer, with predators showing a peak at middle elevations.
Larger-bodied arthropods were more prevalent at higher elevations during winter, while beetles exhibited distinct ecological traits, with larger species peaking at middle elevations.
Details of these trait assignments for each species can be found in Tables S1 and S2.
